questions.stem: Which statement defines a carbohydrate?
options: Any compound whose molecular formula fits Cx(H₂O)y, whatever its structure or source
A polymer made of amino acids that are joined together by peptide links
An ester of propane-1,2,3-triol with three long-chain carboxylic acids
A polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone, or a substance that forms one on hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are defined by structure: several OH groups plus an aldehyde or ketone group, or compounds such as starch that hydrolyse to these. Many carbohydrates fit Cx(H₂O)y, but deoxyribose, C₅H₁₀O₄, does not.

questions.stem: Which compound is a carbohydrate?
options: HOCH₂CH(OH)CHO
HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH
HOOCCH(OH)COOH
CH₃CH(OH)COOH
questions.explanation: HOCH₂CH(OH)CHO has two OH groups and an aldehyde group, so it is a polyhydroxy aldehyde. Propane-1,2,3-triol has no carbonyl group, and the other two contain carboxyl groups rather than an aldehyde or ketone.

questions.stem: Fructose, HOCH₂CO(CHOH)₃CH₂OH, has no aldehyde group. Why is it classed as a carbohydrate?
options: It is a polyhydroxy ketone
Its formula is a hydrate of carbon
It is an isomer of an alcohol
It is a polyhydroxy carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Fructose has a C=O on carbon 2, bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone, together with five OH groups. Polyhydroxy ketones are carbohydrates just as polyhydroxy aldehydes are.

questions.stem: In aqueous solution, how does glucose exist?
options: Only as the open-chain form, because water breaks the ring apart completely
Only as the ring form, because the open-chain form cannot exist at all in water
As glucose ions, because the hydroxyl groups ionise completely in water
As an equilibrium between ring forms and a small amount of the open-chain form
questions.explanation: The ring forms when the OH on carbon 5 adds to the aldehyde group, and this reaction is reversible. In water most glucose is in ring forms, with a small fraction as the open chain.

questions.stem: Glucose in water is mostly in ring forms with no free aldehyde group, yet it gives a positive Tollens test. Which explanation uses equilibrium principles correctly?
options: Tollens reagent converts the ring form into a ketone, which is then oxidised
Only the small amount of chain form reacts, so a mirror forms only at high temperature
The chain form is oxidised, so the equilibrium shifts to replace it until most glucose reacts
The ring form is oxidised directly, because its ring contains an aldehyde group
questions.explanation: As Tollens reagent removes the open-chain aldehyde, the ring-chain equilibrium shifts to produce more chain form, which is oxidised in turn. The ring form itself has no aldehyde group.

questions.stem: What type of reaction joins two glucose molecules to form maltose?
options: Hydrolysis, using up water
Oxidation, releasing hydrogen
Condensation, releasing water
Addition, with no water released
questions.explanation: Two monosaccharides join through a C-O-C link, and an OH from one and an H from the other leave as water. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, which breaks maltose into glucose.

questions.stem: What is the molecular formula of maltose, made from two glucose molecules, C₆H₁₂O₆?
options: C₆H₁₀O₅
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
C₁₂H₂₄O₁₂
C₁₂H₂₀O₁₀
questions.explanation: Two glucose molecules contain C₁₂H₂₄O₁₂, and one water molecule is lost in the condensation, leaving C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. C₁₂H₂₄O₁₂ forgets that water is released.

questions.stem: Three glucose molecules, C₆H₁₂O₆, are joined in a chain by condensation. What is the molecular formula of the trisaccharide?
options: C₁₈H₃₆O₁₈
C₁₈H₃₄O₁₇
C₁₈H₃₂O₁₆
C₁₈H₃₀O₁₅
questions.explanation: Three glucose units contain C₁₈H₃₆O₁₈. Two links form, so two H₂O are lost, giving C₁₈H₃₂O₁₆. Removing three water molecules gives C₁₈H₃₀O₁₅, which would need three links.

questions.stem: Starch is a polymer of glucose. Which formula represents starch?
options: (C₆H₁₂O₅)ₙ
(C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ
(C₆H₁₂O₆)ₙ
(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)ₙ
questions.explanation: Each glucose unit, C₆H₁₂O₆, loses one H₂O as it joins the chain, so the repeating unit is C₆H₁₀O₅. (C₆H₁₂O₆)ₙ would mean no water was lost.

questions.stem: Which carbohydrate is used for energy storage in animals?
options: Starch
Deoxyribose
Glycogen
Cellulose
questions.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen, mainly in the liver and muscles. Plants store energy as starch and use cellulose for structural support; deoxyribose is part of DNA.

questions.stem: Sucrose is hydrolysed in acidic solution. What are the products?
options: Glucose and fructose
Two glucose molecules
Glucose and galactose
Glucose and glycerol
questions.explanation: Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose unit. Maltose gives two glucose molecules, and lactose gives glucose and galactose.

questions.stem: A section of a polysaccharide is hydrolysed completely, and the only product is a single compound with formula C₆H₁₂O₆ containing an aldehyde group. What can be concluded?
options: The polysaccharide is made from glucose and fructose units in alternating order
The polysaccharide is a protein, because hydrolysis gives a single product
The polysaccharide contains ester links, because water was used in hydrolysis
The polysaccharide is made from one type of monomer, an aldohexose such as glucose
questions.explanation: A single hydrolysis product means only one kind of monomer; with an aldehyde group and six carbons it is an aldohexose such as glucose. Fructose has a ketone group, and glycosidic links in carbohydrates are not ester links.

questions.stem: Edible fats and oils are triglycerides. What are they?
options: Esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with three carboxylic acids
Amides of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with three long-chain amines
Polymers of glucose joined by condensation into long branched chains
Long-chain alkanes with three hydroxyl groups along the carbon chain
questions.explanation: Each of the three OH groups of glycerol forms an ester link with the COOH group of a fatty acid. That is why triglycerides undergo the typical ester reactions, such as hydrolysis.

questions.stem: A triglyceride forms from glycerol and three fatty acid molecules. How many water molecules are released?
questions.explanation: Three ester links form, one for each OH group of glycerol, and each condensation releases one water molecule.

questions.stem: Tristearin is made from glycerol, C₃H₈O₃, and three molecules of stearic acid, C₁₇H₃₅COOH. What is its molecular formula?
options: C₅₇H₁₁₀O₆
C₅₇H₁₁₆O₉
C₅₇H₁₁₂O₇
C₅₄H₁₀₈O₆
questions.explanation: Glycerol plus three stearic acids gives C₅₇H₁₁₆O₉. Three water molecules leave, removing H₆O₃, which leaves C₅₇H₁₁₀O₆. C₅₇H₁₁₆O₉ forgets the water lost.

questions.stem: A triglyceride is completely hydrolysed by heating with dilute acid. What are the products?
options: Propane-1,2,3-triol and three carboxylic acid molecules
Propane-1,2,3-triol and three sodium carboxylate ion salts
Glucose and three carboxylic acid molecules
Propan-1-ol and three long-chain alcohol molecules
questions.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis breaks the three ester links, giving glycerol and the three fatty acids. Carboxylate salts form only in alkaline hydrolysis.

questions.stem: How many carbon-carbon double bonds are there in one molecule of linoleic acid, C₁₇H₃₁COOH?
options: Two
One
Three
None
questions.explanation: A saturated acid with a C₁₇ chain would be C₁₇H₃₅COOH. Each C=C removes two hydrogens, and 35 − 31 = 4, so there are two double bonds.

questions.stem: Bromine water is shaken with a sample of olive oil and its orange colour disappears. What does this show?
options: The oil contains carbon-carbon double bonds, which add bromine
The oil contains ester groups, which are oxidised by bromine
The oil is saturated, so bromine dissolves in it without reacting
The oil contains hydroxyl groups, which are replaced by bromine
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across C=C bonds, so the colour disappears as the bromine is used up. Saturated fats do not decolourise bromine quickly.

questions.stem: A fatty acid chain contains -CH₂CH=CHCH₂-. What does this section become after reaction with bromine?
options: -CH₂CH₂CHBrCH₂-
-CHBrCH=CHCHBr-
-CH₂CHBrCHBrCH₂-
-CH₂CBr=CBrCH₂-
questions.explanation: In an addition reaction one bromine atom bonds to each carbon of the double bond, which becomes a single bond. Substituting hydrogen with bromine while keeping the double bond is not what happens.

questions.stem: 0.0100 mol of an oil reacts completely with 4.80 g of bromine, Br₂. Use Br₂ = 160 g mol⁻¹. How many C=C bonds are there in each molecule of the oil?
questions.explanation: n(Br₂) = 4.80 / 160 = 0.0300 mol. Each C=C adds one Br₂, so 0.0300 / 0.0100 = 3 double bonds per molecule. Mistaking Br₂ for Br and using 80 g mol⁻¹ would give six.

questions.stem: 0.00200 mol of a triglyceride reacts completely with 1.016 g of iodine, I₂. Use I₂ = 254 g mol⁻¹. Which description fits the triglyceride?
options: It has one C=C bond per molecule and is unsaturated
It has no C=C bonds, so it is a saturated fat
It has two C=C bonds per molecule and is unsaturated
It has four C=C bonds per molecule and is unsaturated
questions.explanation: n(I₂) = 1.016 / 254 = 0.00400 mol, which is 0.00400 / 0.00200 = 2 mol of I₂ per mole of triglyceride. Each C=C adds one I₂, so there are two double bonds.

questions.stem: Why do unsaturated triglycerides generally have lower melting points than saturated ones of similar size?
options: Unsaturated triglycerides have fewer ester groups, so there are fewer dipole-dipole interactions between them
The cis double bonds put kinks in the chains, so the molecules pack less closely and dispersion forces are weaker
The double bonds make the molecules polar, so they form weaker hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules
The double bonds are weaker than single bonds, so the molecules break apart at a lower temperature on melting
questions.explanation: Kinked chains cannot line up closely, so the dispersion forces between molecules are weaker and less energy is needed to melt them. Melting separates molecules; it does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: In the hydrogenation of a vegetable oil to make a spread, what does the nickel do?
options: It catalyses the addition of hydrogen across C=C bonds
It supplies the hydrogen atoms that add across C=C bonds
It removes water formed by the reaction of the oil
It oxidises the oil so that its melting point rises
questions.explanation: Finely divided nickel provides a surface pathway of lower activation energy for hydrogen addition, and it is not used up. The hydrogen comes from hydrogen gas.

questions.stem: Hydrogenation of an oil is carried out with hydrogen at raised pressure and temperature over a nickel catalyst. What is the purpose of the raised pressure?
options: It increases the activation energy, so only the most reactive C=C bonds are hydrogenated
It lowers the melting point of the oil, so the product stays liquid throughout the process
It forces the nickel to dissolve in the oil, so the catalyst reacts with the double bonds
It increases the concentration of hydrogen, so collisions are more frequent and the rate rises
questions.explanation: Higher pressure means more hydrogen molecules per unit volume, both in the gas and dissolved in the oil, so the rate increases. Pressure does not change activation energy, and the catalyst is not consumed.

questions.stem: A liquid oil is partly hydrogenated. How do its properties change?
options: Fewer C=C bonds remain, so the melting point rises and it becomes more solid
More C=C bonds form, so the melting point rises and it becomes more solid
Fewer C=C bonds remain, so the melting point falls and it becomes more liquid
The ester links are broken, so the product is glycerol and free fatty acids
questions.explanation: Adding hydrogen converts C=C to C-C, straightening the chains so they pack more closely, which raises the melting point. Hydrogenation does not hydrolyse the ester links.

questions.stem: A triglyceride is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. What are the products?
options: Propane-1,2,3-triol and long-chain alcohols
Sodium glyceroxide and three long-chain carboxylic acids
Glucose and sodium carboxylates (soap)
Propane-1,2,3-triol and sodium carboxylates (soap)
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis breaks the ester links, releasing glycerol, and the fatty acids are present as their sodium salts, which are soaps.

questions.stem: A soap anion such as stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻, has two distinct regions. Which description is correct?
options: A hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic carboxylate head
A hydrophilic hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophobic carboxylate head
A hydrophobic carboxylate head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail
A hydrophilic ester head and a hydrophobic hydroxyl tail
questions.explanation: The long non-polar chain interacts with non-polar substances through dispersion forces, while the charged COO⁻ group interacts strongly with water through ion-dipole interactions.

questions.stem: How does a micelle allow oily dirt to be carried away in water?
options: The tails dissolve in the oil while the charged heads face the water, so droplets stay suspended
The heads dissolve in the oil while the hydrocarbon tails face the water, so droplets sink
The soap reacts with the oil to form glycerol, which is soluble in water and is rinsed away
The soap breaks the covalent bonds in the oil, converting it into small polar molecules
questions.explanation: Soap anions cluster around an oil droplet with their non-polar tails in the oil and their negative heads on the outside. The charged surface interacts with water, and the droplets repel each other, so they stay dispersed.

questions.stem: What is the general formula of the amino acids that make up proteins?
options: H₂NCH(R)COOH
H₂NCH₂CH(R)OH
HOCH(R)COOH
H₂NCOCH(R)NH₂
questions.explanation: Each amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, which also carries a hydrogen and a side chain, R. The side chain varies from one amino acid to another.

questions.stem: What forms when glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, self-ionises?
options: H₂NCH₂COO⁻ H⁺
⁺H₃NCH₂COOH₂⁺
⁻HNCH₂COOH
⁺H₃NCH₂COO⁻
questions.explanation: The acidic carboxyl group donates a proton to the basic amino group within the same molecule, giving a species with both a positive and a negative charge. This is why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points.

questions.stem: What is a peptide link?
options: A hydrogen bond between the C=O and N-H of two amino acids
An ionic attraction between two amino acids in a protein
The amide group, -CONH-, joining amino acids in a protein
The ester group, -COO-, joining amino acids in a protein
questions.explanation: Amino acids join by condensation between the COOH of one and the NH₂ of the next, forming an amide group. In proteins this covalent link is called a peptide link.

questions.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, and alanine, H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH, condense so that the carboxyl group of glycine reacts with the amino group of alanine. What dipeptide forms?
options: H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH
H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH
H₂NCH₂COOCH(CH₃)NH₂
HOOCCH₂NHCOCH(CH₃)NH₂
questions.explanation: Glycine's COOH and alanine's NH₂ form the peptide link, so glycine keeps its free NH₂ and alanine keeps its free COOH. H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH is the other dipeptide, formed the opposite way round.

questions.stem: A section of a protein chain is -NHCH(CH₂OH)CONHCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂CO-. Which amino acids are released when this section is hydrolysed?
options: Serine, glycine and lysine
Alanine, glycine and aspartic acid
Serine, alanine and valine
Serine, alanine and glycine
questions.explanation: Each peptide link is broken, so each -NHCH(R)CO- unit becomes H₂NCH(R)COOH. The side chains CH₂OH, CH₃ and H identify serine, alanine and glycine.

questions.stem: In a protein chain, which pair of side chains can form an ionic interaction?
options: -CH₂OH of serine and -CH₂COOH of aspartic acid
-CH₃ of alanine and -(CH₂)₄NH₃⁺ of lysine
-CH₂COO⁻ of aspartic acid and -(CH₂)₄NH₃⁺ of lysine
-CH₃ of alanine and -CH(CH₃)₂ of valine
questions.explanation: An ionic interaction needs oppositely charged groups, such as a carboxylate and a protonated amino group. Non-polar side chains like CH₃ and CH(CH₃)₂ interact through dispersion forces only.

questions.stem: Which secondary interaction holds sections of a protein's main chain together, for example in a helix?
options: Covalent bonds between the C=O of one peptide link and the N-H of another
Ionic interactions between the carbon atoms on the main chain of the protein
Dispersion forces between the oxygen atoms in neighbouring peptide links
Hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide link and the N-H of another
questions.explanation: The N-H hydrogen is partially positive and is attracted to the lone pair of a C=O oxygen on another part of the chain. These are secondary interactions, much weaker than the covalent peptide links.

questions.stem: A water-soluble enzyme folds so that most of its alanine and valine side chains are inside and most of its serine and lysine side chains are on the surface. Why?
options: Non-polar side chains form hydrogen bonds with water, so they move to the inside of the protein
Charged side chains repel water, so they move to the surface where there is less water present
Peptide links are broken and re-formed until the heaviest side chains are near the centre
Polar and charged side chains interact with water, while non-polar side chains interact with each other
questions.explanation: Serine's OH and lysine's NH₃⁺ form hydrogen bonds and ion-dipole interactions with water at the surface. Alanine and valine side chains are non-polar, so they cluster inside, held by dispersion forces.

questions.stem: An enzyme from the stomach works at pH 2, but stops working when placed in a solution at pH 8. Which explanation is best?
options: The high pH hydrolyses all of its peptide links, so the enzyme is broken into separate amino acids
The high pH adds hydroxide ions to its active site, so the substrate is repelled by negative charge
The enzyme is a catalyst, so it is used up more quickly in a basic solution than in an acidic one
Changes in the charges on side chains disrupt ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds, altering the active site
questions.explanation: Changing pH protonates or deprotonates groups such as COOH and NH₂ on side chains. This changes the ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits its substrate.

questions.stem: An enzyme is heated to 80 °C and permanently loses its activity. What happens at the molecular level?
options: The amino acids are oxidised by air, so the side chains form carbon dioxide and water
The enzyme's amino acids self-ionise, so the chain becomes a set of zwitterions
Secondary interactions are disrupted, but the peptide links in the chain remain intact
Peptide links are broken, but the secondary interactions in the chain remain intact
questions.explanation: Increased molecular vibration breaks the weak hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and dispersion forces that hold the folded shape, so the enzyme is denatured. The covalent peptide links are not broken by this heating.
